answer.rationale:
Timing is the strongest signal available: write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, roughly 30 minutes after a release went out 2 hours ago. That temporal alignment makes the new build the leading causal hypothesis, and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a cause rather than a symptom. Failover (b2) moves traffic but carries the same code; capacity (b3) fights a queue that may be growing from a code-level regression; circuit breakers (b4) protect against a failing external dependency, and nothing here points to a partner outage; read-replica routing (b5) helps read pressure on the primary, but the degradation is on the write path, so it is the weakest fit despite being the cheapest.

I am spending my single verification on memory_b1 because it is the memory my intended action rests on most heavily, and its summary is exactly where a dangerous inference could hide. "The rollback finished without customer impact" was recorded on day 18; I do not know the traffic conditions then, and it is entirely plausible that rollback was clean because it happened during a low-volume window. Today we are at daily settlement peak with heavy writes. I also do not know from the summary whether that release carried a schema or data-format migration; a backward-incompatible migration would make rollback the one action that could actually lose customer writes, directly violating the primary objective. I want the original record to tell me the load conditions and whether the rollback path was reversible on the data layer, not just that it "worked."

Memory_b6 supports the shape of the action rather than the action itself: staged gating and canary cohorts surfaced regressions within an hour, which is why I am scoping this as a small guarded test — roll back a limited cohort of write traffic first, watch p99 and write-success on that cohort, and only widen if latency recovers and no writes are dropped. This keeps the blast radius small at peak and preserves the option to abandon the hypothesis.

Uncertainty I am explicitly not collapsing: the three events are concurrent and could be confounded. Peak settlement writes alone could produce this curve, in which case rollback changes nothing and I have burned my single intervention. All six inherited memories are success records with no recorded failures, which is a survivorship-shaped archive — it tells me what worked once, not what the base rates are, and I am treating each as a weak prior rather than a playbook. If b1's source record shows the day-18 rollback happened under light load or involved a migration, I will drop to route_read_replicas or add_capacity as the lower-risk symptom-management play and defer rollback to the next window when write volume falls.
